title: Subnetting You Can Actually See

sources.title: RFC 4632 — Classless Inter-domain Routing
sources.notes: Section3.1: IPv4 prefix notation and address-block sizes including /24 and /26.

sources.title: RFC 3021 — 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links
sources.notes: Section2.1: both addresses are interpreted as host addresses on /31 point-to-point links.

sources.title: RFC 1918 — Address Allocation for Private Internets
sources.notes: Private address range192.168.0.0/16; illustrative addresses are not global Internet destinations.

sections.title: One network, four smaller networks
sections.narration: Divide 192.168.1.0 slash twenty-four into four equal subnets. Instead of guessing decimal boundaries, watch the address space split as two more bits become fixed.
sections.takeaway: Subnetting divides an existing address block into smaller prefix blocks.

sections.title: IPv4 addresses contain thirty-two bits
sections.narration: IPv4 contains thirty-two bits written as four decimal octets. Each octet represents eight binary positions. The dots help humans read the address; they add no bits.
sections.takeaway: Dotted decimal is a readable way to write the underlying bits.

sections.title: A prefix marks the shared beginning
sections.narration: Slash twenty-four fixes the first twenty-four bits. The remaining eight can vary across the block. Changing their values changes addresses while the shared prefix stays constant.
sections.takeaway: The prefix length counts leading network bits, not decimal digits.

sections.title: The mask expresses the boundary
sections.narration: A subnet mask places ones in fixed network positions and zeros in variable positions. For slash twenty-four, three full one-octets followed by zeros produce 255.255.255.0.
sections.takeaway: A contiguous subnet mask and its prefix length describe the same boundary.

sections.title: Find the network with bitwise AND
sections.narration: Bitwise AND preserves bits where the mask is one and clears positions where it is zero. Applying slash twenty-four to address forty-two produces network 192.168.1.0.
sections.takeaway: Masking an address identifies the prefix block that contains it.

sections.title: Count the parent block
sections.narration: Eight variable bits allow two to the eighth combinations: 256 addresses. Their final octet runs from zero through 255. Total addresses and usable host addresses are different counts.
sections.takeaway: Count all addresses before applying ordinary LAN host reservations.

sections.title: Borrow two bits for four subnets
sections.narration: One added prefix bit splits the block in half. Another splits those halves again. Two borrowed bits give four combinations, so our new subnet prefix is twenty-six.
sections.takeaway: Extending a prefix creates smaller blocks within the original block.

sections.title: Build the slash-twenty-six mask
sections.narration: The last mask octet now begins with two ones: 128 plus 64 equals 192. The six remaining zeros mark host positions in mask 255.255.255.192.
sections.takeaway: Two leading ones in the last octet make the /26 boundary.

sections.title: Six host bits make sixty-four addresses
sections.narration: Each slash-twenty-six subnet has six variable bits, creating sixty-four total addresses. Four blocks of sixty-four exactly cover the parent’s 256 addresses without gaps or overlap.
sections.takeaway: The four /26 blocks exactly cover the original /24.

sections.title: The four binary prefixes
sections.narration: Cycle the borrowed bits through zero-zero, zero-one, one-zero, and one-one. With host bits cleared, the aligned network octets become zero, sixty-four, 128, and 192.
sections.takeaway: Aligned /26 network starts are separated by 64 addresses.

sections.title: Subnet one: zero through sixty-three
sections.narration: The first subnet covers zero through sixty-three. Ordinary LAN conventions reserve zero as the network address and sixty-three as broadcast, leaving host addresses one through sixty-two.
sections.takeaway: Subnet one contains 64 total addresses and 62 ordinary host addresses.

sections.title: Subnet two: sixty-four through 127
sections.narration: The second subnet spans sixty-four through 127. Its ordinary hosts are sixty-five through 126. A broadcast address need not end in 255; the prefix determines its role.
sections.takeaway: Network and broadcast roles depend on the prefix, not just the last octet.

sections.title: Subnet three: 128 through 191
sections.narration: The third subnet begins at 128 and ends at 191. Preserve its borrowed prefix bits while varying the six host bits. Ordinary host addresses are 129 through 190.
sections.takeaway: Clear host bits while preserving the complete 26-bit network prefix.

sections.title: Subnet four: 192 through 255
sections.narration: The fourth subnet begins at 192 and ends at 255. Its ordinary hosts are 193 through 254. Together all four ranges cover the original block exactly once.
sections.takeaway: Nonoverlapping contiguous ranges verify the subdivision.

sections.title: Locate the host ending in seventy
sections.narration: Seventy in binary is 01000110. AND it with the final mask octet 11000000 and obtain sixty-four. Address 192.168.1.70 therefore belongs to subnet 192.168.1.64/26.
sections.takeaway: A range check and a mask operation should identify the same subnet.

sections.title: Same prefix or a different subnet?
sections.narration: Seventy and one hundred both mask to subnet sixty-four. Address 130 masks to 128 instead. Compare the complete masked prefix, rather than judging by similar-looking decimal addresses.
sections.takeaway: Compare masked network prefixes, using the relevant mask.

sections.title: Remote destinations use a router
sections.narration: A host ordinarily reaches destinations in its own subnet locally. For another subnet it chooses an appropriate next-hop router. A prefix boundary changes the forwarding decision, not physical location.
bullets: Remote subnet: use a next-hop router
sections.takeaway: A gateway connects networks that have different prefixes.

sections.title: Choose a prefix for fifty hosts
sections.narration: An ordinary slash-twenty-seven LAN offers thirty usable addresses, too few for fifty hosts. Slash twenty-six provides sixty-two, making it the smallest equal block meeting this requirement.
sections.takeaway: Choose enough host bits for the requirement and reserved addresses.

sections.title: More prefix bits, fewer addresses
sections.narration: Fix one more bit and halve the block. Slash twenty-five contains 128 addresses, slash twenty-six sixty-four, and slash twenty-seven thirty-two. The number of variable bits explains the direction.
sections.takeaway: Every additional fixed bit halves the number of address combinations.

sections.title: The subtract-two rule has exceptions
sections.narration: Subtracting two is an ordinary LAN convention, not a universal rule. Appropriately configured slash-thirty-one point-to-point links use both addresses; slash thirty-two denotes one specific address.
sections.takeaway: The total-address formula is general; host usability depends on context.

sections.title: A subnet is not a security policy
sections.narration: Subnetting organizes addresses and routing. It does not automatically encrypt traffic or enforce isolation. Packets can cross subnet boundaries whenever the configured routing and access policies allow them.
sections.takeaway: A prefix boundary does not replace a security policy.

sections.title: CIDR replaces the classful shortcut
sections.narration: Do not infer a default class from the first octet. Modern classless addressing uses the stated prefix. Our 192.168.1 examples are private addresses, not globally routable destinations.
sections.takeaway: Read the actual prefix instead of guessing an old default class.

sections.title: Check all four answers
sections.narration: Check starts zero, sixty-four, 128, 192 and broadcasts sixty-three, 127, 191, 255. Each range has sixty-four addresses. Verify alignment, coverage, and nonoverlap before assigning hosts.
bullets: Each ordinary LAN has 62 host slots
sections.takeaway: Verify alignment, size, boundaries, and coverage before assigning addresses.

sections.title: Move the boundary, solve the puzzle
sections.narration: Borrowing two bits made four slash-twenty-six subnets. Six host bits remain in each. Binary boundaries, AND, and address combinations explain the answer without memorizing a subnet table.
sections.takeaway: Subnetting follows directly from fixed prefixes and variable address bits.
